units.translation: And the down is just now coming over his cheeks, as the season of youth blooms.
having this season that turns mortals back.
The tree-bearing season from the moistening marriage is complete.
seasonable, ripe
seasonable, ripe.
i.e. entered into at the mature age for marriage.
First I pour libations to Zeus of the ripe marriage, and the second mixing I assign to the heroes,
Orithyia
A tragedy of Aeschylus was entitled Orithyia, of which one fragment (280) survives.

That Sophocles wrote a tragedy of the same name cannot be inferred from the words of John Siceliotes cited on Aeschylus frag. 280: on this Wilamowitz spoke in Hermes vol. 10 p. 334. Orithyia was the daughter of Erechtheus, whom Boreas snatched from Attica and carried off to Thrace, and by him she bore Zetes and Calais: see Thes. vol. 8 p. 2064.
as

It has the force of a preposition, adverb, and conjunction: hence certain grammarians have invented thirty meanings for it, which in fact reduce to a few, as is shown in Thes. vol. 8 p. 2077-2106. No examples of the preposition (to, into), which is construed with the accusative, are found in Aeschylus, but there are not a few of the adverb and conjunction.
ὡς as an adverb, serving for comparison of two persons or things, corresponds to the Latin particles ut, sicut, velut, quemadmodum, tanquam.
ὡς placed after the thing compared is written with an accent
ὡς is used for quam after a comparative instead of ἤ
ὡς, preceded by τοιόσδε, τόσος.
ὡς used relatively, how, in what way.
ὡς in an adverbial clause, as, in what way.
ὡς joined with adverbs
ὡς with the superlative, quam.
ὡς indicating the reason why someone thinks something about a matter, or seems to another to think, as, as if, thinking.
ὡς with a participle, as one who, as if.
With genitive absolutes
ὡς the same as ὅτι, which the Latins express by the accusative with infinitive.
With the optative in indirect speech.
ὡς in final clauses and those indicating purpose is the same as ὅπως.
ὡς ἄν final with the subjunctive.
ὡς final with the optative after past tenses in indirect speech
ὡς with the infinitive.
Without the infinitive
ὡς i.q. ὥστε so that.
ὡς i.q. ἐπεί, to which the Latin quippe, quandoquidem, quoniam, nam correspond.
ὡς with temporal meaning, just as the Latins also use the particle ut, on which see Thes. vol. 8 p. 2089.
ὡς in exclamation, how, quam.
ὡς δή ironic exclamation.

ὡς (adverb oxytone or, according to the opinion of the ancient grammarians, perispomenon ὡς, on which see Thes. vol. 8 p. 2083) i.q. οὕτως thus, frequent in epic poets, rare in Attic, who use it in certain fixed formulas, οὐδ᾽ ὥς, ἀλλ' ὡς, and a few others.
